items.title: Predictors of Return to Work Following Major Trauma in New Zealand.
items.authors: Finlayson D, Logan S, Jemberie D, Quinn N, Joyce LR, Wakeman C, McCombie A.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This study aimed to identify physical and psychological predictors of return to work (RTW) in a cohort of major trauma patients in New Zealand.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A retrospective cohort study was conducted at Christchurch Hospital involving patients identified from the New Zealand Major Trauma Registry. Full-time workers (n = 130) who sustained major trauma between 2016 and 2020 completed self-reported questionnaires assessing post-injury work capacity, PTSD (PCL-5), anxiety and depression (HADS) and perceived social support (MSPSS). Univariable and multivariable analyses were performed to determine predictors of decreased RTW following injury.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Older age, longer hospital length of stay (LOS) and ICU admission were all significantly associated with decreased RTW in the univariable analysis. Probable anxiety and depression were also significantly associated with decreased RTW, while meeting PTSD thresholds did not yield a significant association. In the final multivariable analysis, older age (OR 1.08, p < 0.01), longer LOS (OR 1.04, p = 0.048) and those with probable depression (OR 5.29, p = 0.01) were significantly associated with decreased RTW.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Probable depression is a strong, independent psychological predictor of reduced RTW following major trauma. These findings highlight the need for integrated post-trauma care models that incorporate routine psychological screening and early intervention to address both the physical and psychological needs of patients suffering from major trauma.

items.title: An oral-origin Streptococcus salivarius associated with schizophrenia reshapes intestinal T-cell immunity and promotes IL-17A-dominated inflammation.
items.authors: Kang Y, Fan Y, Ma Q, Yu L, Liu J, Liu Y, Zhou Z, Zhao H, Yang Z, Xun Y, Jia M, Zhao B, Ma X, Wang W, Guo Y.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Emerging evidence suggests that oral microbial dysbiosis contributes to neuropsychiatric disorders through microbiome-immune interactions. We previously identified an oral-origin Streptococcus salivarius enriched in individuals with schizophrenia (SCZ) and demonstrated its ability to become enriched in the intestine after oral administration. However, whether this disease-associated bacterium remodels host adaptive immunity remains unclear. Here, we investigated the effects of S. salivarius on intestinal CD4^+ T-cell homeostasis and inflammatory responses.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Male C57BL/6 mice were orally administered S. salivarius for 14 days with or without prior antibiotic-mediated depletion of resident microbiota. Intestinal enrichment of S. salivarius was confirmed by quantitative PCR. Colonic lamina propria mononuclear cells (LPMCs) and mesenteric lymph node (MLN) cells were analyzed using single-cell RNA sequencing and flow cytometry to characterize CD4^+ T cell responses. Cytokine levels in colon tissues and serum were quantified by ELISA.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Single-cell transcriptomic analysis demonstrated that intestinal enrichment of S. salivarius altered Treg-associated transcriptional programs, with reduced Treg-stability signatures and increased Type-17-associated features. Flow cytometry confirmed increased Th17 cells, reduced Treg frequencies, and disruption of intestinal Th17/Treg homeostasis. Similar immune alternations were observed in MLNs, indicating extension of gut-associated immune remodeling beyond the intestinal mucosa. S. salivarius exposure was further associated with selective IL-17A in colonic tissues and serum, whereas IL-6, IL-1β, IL-10, and TGF-β remained largely unchanged. Comparable immune changes were observed in both antibiotic-pretreated and conventional SPF mice, indicating that these immunological effects were not restricted to microbiota-depletion condition.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: These findings identify an SCZ-associated oral-origin S. salivarius as a modulator of intestinal adaptive immunity. Intestinal enrichment of S. salivarius was associated with coordinated remodeling of Treg-associated transcriptional programs, Th17-biased immune polarization, and an IL-17A-dominated inflammatory response, Together, these results define an intestinal immune mechanism through which a disease-associated oral bacterium may contribute to oral-gut immune interactions and provide experimental support for one immunological component of the oral-gut-brain axis relevant to schizophrenia.

items.title: Job Coaching and Smartphone-Based Cognitive Behavioral Techniques for Returning to Work and Coping With Unemployment (DRIVEN): Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.authors: Griffith JW, Letkiewicz AM, Saturday ML, Graham AK, Alperin K, Danielson EC, Levit A, Shankman SA.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Unemployment has economic consequences and is associated with emotional distress and impairment. Joblessness is often associated with depression, leading to a vicious cycle of reduced drive to seek work, deepening financial stress, and worsening depression. Few scalable interventions exist that integrate job-search strategies with cognitive behavioral techniques.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: The study aimed to determine the efficacy of a Distress-Informed Return-to-Work Intervention (DRIVEN). The primary hypothesis was that DRIVEN would be more efficacious than the control condition in improving job-search behavior. Secondary analyses examined job attainment, depression, and positive affect.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A randomized controlled trial was conducted from August 2023 to September 2024. Assessments were at baseline, weeks 1 through 6, and 8 and 16 weeks postintervention. Participants were a nationwide sample of unemployed job seekers aged 18 years or older who had never earned more than US $100,000 in a year. Participants received either (1) DRIVEN, which included 6 weeks of cognitive behavioral exercises in a mobile app combined with three 1-hour coaching sessions over videoconference or (2) emailed articles containing job-search advice. Primary outcome measures were subscales of a modified Job Search Behavior Scale (preparatory and active job search). Secondary outcomes included job attainment and mental health outcomes.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Participants were a nationwide sample (N=126; mean age 33.6, SD 6.6 y), including 62 (49.2%) females. During the acute treatment phase, mixed-effects linear models showed that for DRIVEN, preparatory job-search behavior increased by an estimated 0.053 (95% CI 0.031-0.076) units per day from baseline, which was a larger effect than in the control condition (0.011, 95% CI -0.011 to 0.033 units per day; P =.008). Active job-search behavior increased by 0.061 (95% CI 0.038-0.084) units per day from baseline, which was significantly larger than in the control group (point estimate: 0.025, 95% CI 0.001-0.047; P =.03). Depression decreased more in the DRIVEN group vs control (DRIVEN point estimate=-0.214, 95% CI -0.255 to -0.172 vs control group point estimate=-0.122, 95% CI -0.163 to -0.081; P =.002), and participants were more likely to get a job in the DRIVEN group (68.3% vs 50.8%; P =.046). Self-report outcomes did not significantly differ during the follow-up periods.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: DRIVEN was superior to emailed job-search advice for the primary outcome (job-search behavior) and secondary outcomes (job attainment, depression, and positive affect). This intervention may be beneficial for distressed unemployed individuals seeking work.

items.title: Functional connectivity of anterior cingulate cortex subregions in suicidal ideation in major depression: circuit mechanisms, exploratory classification, and treatment-related changes.
items.authors: Jing Y, Jing L, Chen X, Xu J, Li D, Li R, Li X, Liu J, Zhang X, Zhou J, Wang G.

sections.text: Suicidal ideation (SI) is a critical challenge in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet its precise neural circuitry remains elusive. Although anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is implicated, its subregional roles remain poorly understood. This study aimed to delineate SI-specific neural circuitry by examining whole-brain functional connectivity (FC) of ACC subregions: subgenual ACC (sgACC), pregenual ACC (pgACC), and dorsal ACC (dACC). Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data were analyzed from 237 MDD patients (109 with SI [MDD-SI], 128 without SI [MDD-NSI]) and 152 healthy controls (HCs) at baseline. Group assignment relied on lifetime SI (trait-like SI) from the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale, with current SI (state-like SI) measured by the suicide item of 17-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale. Of these, 129 MDD patients underwent 8-week follow-up scanning after treatment. Cross-sectional analysis identified two SI-specific FC alterations: left pgACC-right precuneus and left dACC-left fusiform connectivity. These FCs were enhanced in MDD-SI compared to MDD-NSI, showed no differences between MDD-NSI and HCs, and correlated with trait-like SI severity. An exploratory model incorporating these FCs and clinical covariates achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.723 for trait-like SI identification. Longitudinally, the baseline elevation in left pgACC-right precuneus FC normalized after treatment specifically in MDD-SI, and this reduction paralleled the decrease in state-like SI severity. Our findings clarify ACC subregion-specific SI mechanisms, provide an exploratory evaluation of trait-like SI identification and identify a potential state-like SI therapeutic circuit. Collectively, this work translates vague ACC abnormality into localizable circuits, advancing precision neuroscience for MDD-SI.

items.title: Controlled postoperative red wine intake versus abstinence in habitual wine drinkers undergoing elective urological surgery (WISE): a translational randomized controlled trial assessing quality of life, surgical outcomes and complications.
items.authors: Capitanio U, Basile G, Barrasso C, Derevianko A, Musso G, Cei F, Disabato N, Re C, Belladelli F, Piccolo C, Rosiello G, Canibus D, Trevisani F, Larcher A, Salonia A, Bettiga A, Ratti MM, Montorsi F.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: To date, no prospective randomized study has evaluated whether controlled postoperative red wine intake, compared with abstinence, affects recovery in habitual wine drinkers undergoing surgery.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this single-center randomized controlled trial (NCT05261620), habitual wine drinkers scheduled for elective urological surgery were randomized 1:1 to abstinence from alcohol (Control Arm) or standardized red wine intake (150 mL of 13% v/v red wine with lunch and with dinner) from postoperative day 1 to day 30 (Experimental Arm). The primary endpoint was the between-group difference in change from baseline to 30 days in the SF-36 Mental Health Index (MHI). Secondary endpoints included postoperative complications, hospital readmission, length of hospitalization, blood parameters, and oxidative stress markers.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The mean change in MHI was - 0.6 in the Control Arm and + 0.7 in the Experimental Arm (difference 1.3 points; 95% CI - 1.9 to 4.6; p = 0.4). Overall complications (16.1% vs. 9.8%; p = 0.4), length of hospital stay and 30-day readmissions (8.1% vs. 0%; p = 0.06) did not differ significantly between the Control and Experimental Arms, respectively. Blood parameters and oxidative stress markers showed no clinically relevant differences.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Among predominantly older male habitual wine drinkers undergoing elective urological surgery, controlled postoperative red wine intake did not improve 30-day quality of life compared with abstinence. Complications and blood parameters did not differ meaningfully. These findings do not support the initiation or promotion of alcohol use.

sections.heading: Trial registration
sections.text: This study was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT05261620, registered on 02/20/2022. https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05261620 ).

items.title: Association between brain functional state indices and eye movement features in patients with anxiety disorders: a cross-sectional study.
items.authors: Zhang W, Wang J, Xu Z.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This study systematically examined the differences in brain functional states and eye movement performance among patients with anxiety disorder and explored their associations using real-world data.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A total of 195 patients with anxiety disorders were enrolled between January 2023 and June 2024. Psychological assessments included SAS (Self-Rating Anxiety Scale) and PSQI (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index) instruments. Brain functional indices and eye movement parameters (prosaccade task, antisaccade task and smooth-pursuit task) were collected. Group comparisons, correlation analyses, and logistic regression models were employed to evaluate the contributions and predictive performance of these markers.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Patients showed significantly lower Brain Inhibition, Stability, and Emptying Indices, and higher Emotion Resistance and Anxiety Tendency Indices. Eye movement tests revealed prolonged latencies and completion times in prosaccade and antisaccade tasks. Significant correlations were observed between brain functional state indices and eye movement performance. The eye-movement-based model yielded a higher area under the curve (AUC) (0.895) than the brain-function-based model (AUC = 0.621).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Combined brain functional and eye movement indices may serve as objective, adjunctive measures for the assessment of anxiety disorders, reflecting underlying neural dysregulation.

items.title: Sex differences in associations between sleep architecture and CBC-derived immune cell indices in MDD with comorbid insomnia.
items.authors: Wang Q, Deng M, Wang Y, Gu D, Zhu W, Chen L, Wang J, Luan P.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Insomnia symptoms and alterations in sleep architecture are core pathophysiological features of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD). While sex differences in MDD prevalence and symptomatology are well documented, the specific interplay between sleep architecture and complete blood count (CBC)-derived immune cell indices, metabolic markers, and thyroid-related parameters remains under-characterized with respect to sex.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study included 126 patients with MDD and comorbid insomnia (43 males, 83 females). All participants underwent overnight polysomnography (PSG) and fasting blood biochemical analysis. Sex-specific associations between objective sleep parameters and peripheral biomarkers were analyzed using age-adjusted partial Spearman correlation and multiple linear regression models with interaction terms.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Female patients had longer REM sleep latency and N2 sleep duration, whereas male patients had a higher apnea-hypopnea index. Females had higher HDL-C levels, while males had higher monocyte counts. In age-adjusted FDR-corrected correlation analyses, significant associations involving CBC-derived immune cell counts were observed primarily in male patients, where lymphocyte count was associated with TST, REM sleep duration, N1%, and N2 sleep duration; no significant CBC-derived immune cell count correlations remained in female patients. sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: These findings suggest that sex may shape both the subjective-objective expression of sleep disturbance and lymphocyte-related sleep regulation in patients with MDD and comorbid insomnia. The pattern of poorer subjective sleep quality despite relatively favorable selected PSG characteristics in females, together with sex-dependent lymphocyte associations involving REM sleep and arousal measures, warrants further validation in larger longitudinal studies.

items.title: Plasma Lipidomic Features of Adolescent Major Depressive Disorder and Lipid Changes After Fluoxetine Treatment.
items.authors: Liu C, Li Y, Hou H, Guo J, Qin B, Xu X, He Y, Lei T, Chen F, Zhang L, Liu Q, Gao L, Shi J, Xing H, Teng T, Qiu T, Zhou X.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) in adolescents is a major public health concern, yet objective biological markers and treatment-related metabolic changes remain insufficiently understood. This study aimed to characterize plasma lipidomic alterations in adolescent MDD and explore lipid changes associated with fluoxetine treatment.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study enrolled 75 adolescents with MDD and 75 matched healthy controls (HCs). Among the adolescents with MDD, 44 had paired baseline and week-8 plasma samples available and were included in the longitudinal analysis. Plasma lipidomic profiles were analyzed using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 865 lipid species were detected. Compared with HCs, adolescents with MDD showed distinct plasma lipidomic profiles, with 82 differentially abundant lipid species identified, primarily involving triglycerides, lysophospholipids, free fatty acids, membrane phospholipids, and sphingolipids. Among the machine-learning models, logistic regression showed the highest discriminative performance, with a pooled out-of-fold AUC of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.79-0.91). Longitudinal analysis identified 21 lipid species meeting the differential criteria following fluoxetine treatment, mainly involving triglycerides and bile acid-related metabolites. Integrative pathway and target analyses suggested that fluoxetine-associated lipid changes may involve neurotransmitter signaling, inflammatory lipid metabolism, PI3K-Akt signaling, and nuclear receptor-related pathways.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This study characterizes alterations in plasma lipid metabolism in adolescent MDD and the lipidomic changes following fluoxetine treatment, providing new lipidomic evidence for candidate lipid signatures and potential treatment-associated biological pathways.

sections.heading: Trial registration
sections.text: ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT05814640. Registered 20 February 2023, https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05814640.

items.title: Delayed Recognition of Autism Spectrum Disorder and Off-Label Lurasidone After Intolerance to Risperidone and Aripiprazole in a Latin American Child: A Case Report.
items.authors: Orellana Banegas L, Urbina R, Flores Antúnez YII, Mejia JA.

sections.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) can be difficult to recognize when co-occurring psychiatric symptoms are more clinically prominent, which may delay diagnosis. We report the case of a nine-year-old Latin American boy whose ASD and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) were not diagnosed until approximately 27 months after initial presentation with irritability, mood lability, anxiety, and, subsequently, hallucinatory experiences; these symptoms were initially managed as primary psychiatric conditions. During this interval, fluoxetine was discontinued due to symptom worsening, sertraline produced only partial benefit, and both Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved agents for irritability associated with autistic disorder were discontinued because of adverse effects: risperidone due to significant weight gain and aripiprazole due to nausea, vomiting, and dizziness. A detailed neurodevelopmental reassessment subsequently identified longstanding social communication difficulties, rigid routines, sensory sensitivities, and restricted interests, supporting diagnoses of ASD and OCD. Low-dose lurasidone (20 mg nightly) was initiated off-label alongside continued sertraline. Over the following year, the patient demonstrated sustained improvement in irritability, aggression, self-injurious behavior, anxiety, and sleep disturbance. Hallucinatory experiences resolved within approximately three months and did not recur, with no significant adverse effects observed. This case illustrates how more prominent psychiatric symptoms can mask ASD and describes the individualized use of off-label lurasidone after intolerance to approved agents. However, the temporal association with clinical improvement does not establish causality, and findings from a single case cannot demonstrate efficacy.

items.title: Does Reconstructive Surgery Improve Psychological Recovery After Burn Injury?
items.authors: Gravino D, Attard K.

sections.text: Burn reconstruction aims to restore function, comfort, and appearance, but its effect on psychological recovery remains less certain. This narrative review aimed to examine depression, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), demoralization, body image, social participation, post-traumatic growth (PTG), neurocognitive recovery, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL) after burn reconstruction. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched from inception to September 17, 2026, with citation chaining and targeted searches for reconstructive modalities and validated outcome instruments. The evidence is heterogeneous and predominantly observational. Contracture release and laser scar treatment consistently improve selected functional, symptom, and burn-specific quality-of-life outcomes. Autologous fat grafting is promising for scar quality and satisfaction, but comparative evidence remains limited. In contrast, large Burn Model System analyses do not demonstrate consistent improvements in broad mental-health scores among survivors undergoing later surgery; these adjusted associations identify ongoing vulnerability but do not establish that reconstruction causes psychological harm. Depression, anxiety, PTSD, demoralization, body-image distress, and cognitive impairment should therefore be measured as distinct outcomes rather than inferred from scar appearance or generic HRQoL. The most defensible model is one of integrated care: reconstructive surgery combined with rehabilitation, trauma-informed communication, realistic expectation setting, psychological screening, active follow-up, and timely mental-health referral. Future studies should use procedure-specific preoperative baselines, repeated assessments, appropriate comparators, Burn Care Quality Platform (BCQP) variables, and validated burn-specific participation and scar-impact measures.

items.title: Hierarchical affective predictive imbalance in adolescent borderline personality disorder: task-evoked fMRI evidence from multimodal machine learning.
items.authors: Ma M, Wang X, Tan Z, Liu J, Xiao Q, Hu T, Grecucci A, Yi X.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Predictive-processing accounts of BPD, including the hierarchical-prior-imbalance account proposed by Herzog, offer a framework for interpreting affective instability and impulsivity. The present task-fMRI study evaluates whether discriminative task-evoked patterns are consistent with this framework; because it does not directly estimate prediction errors, precision weighting, or hierarchical belief updating, it is not a mechanistic test of predictive processing.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: To evaluate this question, this study developed a leakage-controlled multimodal machine learning framework for individualized classification of adolescents with BPD and healthy controls based on emotional Go/No-Go task-fMRI activity. Three feature domains were constructed: functional connectivity (FC), task-evoked general linear model (GLM)-derived temporal features, and clinical variables. Seven feature settings, including single-modality, dual-modality, and full multimodal combinations, were evaluated using multiple conventional machine learning classifiers, including logistic regression, support vector machine, k-nearest neighbors, Gaussian naive Bayes, multilayer perceptron, random forest, and XGBoost or gradient boosting.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The results showed that task-evoked GLM-derived features provided the strongest single-modality discriminative information (AUC of 0.881 ± 0.055). SHAP analysis confirmed the predominance of GLM-derived features, accounting for 83.1% of total model attribution, compared to 9.5 and 7.5% for functional connectivity and clinical variables, respectively. At the neural level, discriminative features were distributed across visual/perceptual regions (calcarine, cuneus, occipital cortex), temporoparietal/default-mode hubs (angular and supramarginal gyri), frontal control regions (inferior frontal gyrus), and subcortical structures (putamen). This distributed pattern aligns with a hierarchical organization spanning perceptual input, contextual/self-referential processing, and top-down inhibitory control systems, consistent with the proposed model of hierarchical affective predictive imbalance.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Task-evoked GLM-derived features were the primary source of discriminative information for adolescent BPD, with functional connectivity and clinical variables providing modest additional value. The resulting classification pattern is consistent with hierarchical predictive-processing accounts but does not establish a specific predictive-processing mechanism. The same regional pattern may also reflect visual attention, salience processing, and executive inhibitory control.

items.title: Redox compromise as an early, modifiable entry point in schizophrenia: a staging framework for early intervention.
items.authors: Lado LA, Misir A.

sections.text: Schizophrenia is understood as a disorder of dopamine signaling and is treated with dopamine receptor antagonists. These drugs reduce hallucinations and delusions but leave cognitive impairment, negative symptoms and functional decline largely untouched. This article advances a complementary view, as a hypothesis rather than an established account. It treats redox compromise, meaning chronic oxidative stress, glutathione depletion, mitochondrial inefficiency and the inflammatory state that accompanies them, as an early and modifiable point of entry into a self-reinforcing loop. The loop also involves NMDA receptor hypofunction, impairment of parvalbumin interneurons, disturbed circuit connectivity and, last, the dopaminergic phenotype that current drugs address. It runs in both directions: blocking NMDA receptors itself generates oxidative stress in animal models, so the claim is not that redox compromise comes first, but that it can be measured and modified early, before the changes that current treatment cannot reverse. The clinical staging framework of McGorry and the neuroprogression framework of Berk provide the architecture for translating this into intervention windows, with the first two levels treated as risk strata rather than disease stages. Impaired glucose tolerance in first-episode patients who have never taken antipsychotics, which neither medication nor chronicity can explain, is presented as evidence that metabolic disturbance is a parallel expression of the same systemic process. The progressive framing is contested. The principal counterevidence, including the contribution of antipsychotic exposure to brain volume loss and the largely stable course of cognitive impairment after onset, is set out together with the results that would require abandoning it. We organize the biomarker literature by stage and propose three predictions that a trial could refute: that biomarker-stratified prevention will outperform unselected prevention at the clinical high-risk stage; that medial prefrontal glutathione and mismatch negativity deficit will add predictive value beyond clinical assessment; and that removing the redox measures from a multimodal panel will worsen its prediction of transition. A biomarker-stratified phase 2b trial with a formal power calculation is proposed. The human evidence supports association and biological plausibility rather than proven causal direction.

items.title: Association between social media use, social appearance anxiety, and eating disorder risk in adolescents.
items.authors: Özkan GÖ, Yüce MN, Karagöl B.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: This study aimed to examine the relationships between social media use and social appearance anxiety, eating behavior, and eating disorders in adolescents.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this study, a questionnaire including the social media use scale, social appearance anxiety scale, and eating disorder assessment questionnaire-short form was administered face-to-face to 309 adolescents.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: In total, 47.2% of participants were girls and 52.8% were boys, with an average age of 16.0 ± 0.9 years. The most commonly used social media applications are WhatsApp (83.2%) and Instagram (81.2%). The mean social appearance anxiety score of the girls (38.1 ± 16.8) was higher than that of the boys (30.8 ± 13.9). There was a positive relationship between social appearance anxiety and continuity of social media use, as well as the risk of eating disorders ( p  < 0.05). There was also a positive relationship between social media use continuity and the risk of eating disorders ( p  < 0.05). The continuous use of social media increased the likelihood of social appearance anxiety ( β  = 0.963, 95% CI: 0.520-1.406); increased anxiety about social appearance was associated with a higher likelihood of developing an eating disorder ( β  = 0.068, %95 CI: 0.053-0.083) ( p  < 0.05).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Increased social media use in adolescents is associated with higher levels of social appearance anxiety and an increased risk of eating disorders. Educating adolescents about social media use may help reduce the incidence of eating disorders.

items.title: Digital attention disruption and academic impact in adolescents: a data-driven network and machine learning analysis.
items.authors: Liu Y.

sections.text: Academic impact associated with digital media use is a topic of considerable concern in the fields of adolescent mental health and education; however, the role of attention status in this context remains largely unknown. The present study aimed to systematically investigate the multidimensional association patterns between attention-related characteristics and academic impact among adolescents using data mining approaches. The data were derived from two publicly available cross-sectional survey datasets, and a final sample of 799 adolescents aged 19 years and below was included after age screening. The analytical framework integrated LASSO regression, regularized partial correlation network analysis based on EBICglasso, XGBoost predictive modeling with SHAP interpretation, and latent profile analysis. Results showed that LASSO regression identified stress level (coefficient = 0.384) and social media use duration (coefficient = 0.297) as the strongest predictors of academic impact. Network analysis revealed a three-community structure, corresponding to the "digital distraction load," "psychological-academic exhaustion," and "academic engagement" dimensions, with academic impact located at the intersection of the first two communities. The XGBoost model achieved an AUC of 0.842, and SHAP dependence plots further revealed a nonlinear pattern with an inflection point at approximately 3.5 hours for daily social media use duration and a nonlinear effect of stress level. Latent profile analysis identified three subgroups, among which the "high stress-exhaustion" group showed a probability of academic impact as high as 79.4%. These findings indicate that attention-related characteristics can effectively predict academic impact status in adolescents, with stress level, social media use duration, and number of notifications constituting the most influential set of predictors. The results provide data-driven theoretical evidence and practical implications for the early identification and stratified intervention of academic impact in adolescents.

items.title: Nature-based mindfulness program for parents and caregivers: a mixed-methods study.
items.authors: Jiwen Zhang Z, Lo HHM, Lok WF, Chen QR.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: There is a growing interest in incorporating nature into mindfulness-based programs. This study is unique as it targets parents and family caregivers experiencing caregiving stress.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A mixed-methods study was conducted to evaluate the outcome of a nature-based mindfulness intervention program. A comprehensive outcome measures targeting benefits of parents and caregivers, including mental health symptoms, wellbeing, physical distress, family functioning, and family conflicts, were assessed over time. The role of nature in overall outcome was investigated through the participants' perceived connectedness to nature and time spent in nature. The program consists of four sessions, totaling 8 h of contact time, held at a retreat center and social care units. A total of 95 participants were recruited, including 40 caregivers of older adults and 55 parents under stress. The study employed a time series design, with assessments conducted 1 month before the program, pre-program, post-program, and at a 3-month follow-up.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: For caregivers, significant improvements were observed in multiple outcome measures, including anxiety, stress, physical distress, daily functioning, and wellbeing, following the program. Further improvement in connectedness with nature was noted between the pre-test and the 3-month follow-up, with depression and family functioning approaching significance. For parents under stress, significant improvements were found only in wellbeing after the program. However, additional improvements in anxiety, stress, physical distress, and family conflicts (psychological aggression, corporal punishment, and physical maltreatment) were observed during the follow-up period, with depression and daily functioning approaching significance. Hierarchical regression analysis indicated that connectedness to nature significantly associated with the program's effect on depression. Qualitative analysis revealed that participants benefited from attention restoration, increased awareness, and insights gained from nature and mindfulness practices.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Due to the limitations of the study, including the lack of control group and the use of self-reported measures, future study should verify the benefits of nature-based mindfulness programs particularly on the effects on parents and caregivers under stress and at risk of mental health conditions.

abstract.text:
There is a growing interest in incorporating nature into mindfulness-based programs. This study is unique as it targets parents and family caregivers experiencing caregiving stress.

A mixed-methods study was conducted to evaluate the outcome of a nature-based mindfulness intervention program. A comprehensive outcome measures targeting benefits of parents and caregivers, including mental health symptoms, wellbeing, physical distress, family functioning, and family conflicts, were assessed over time. The role of nature in overall outcome was investigated through the participants' perceived connectedness to nature and time spent in nature. The program consists of four sessions, totaling 8 h of contact time, held at a retreat center and social care units. A total of 95 participants were recruited, including 40 caregivers of older adults and 55 parents under stress. The study employed a time series design, with assessments conducted 1 month before the program, pre-program, post-program, and at a 3-month follow-up.

For caregivers, significant improvements were observed in multiple outcome measures, including anxiety, stress, physical distress, daily functioning, and wellbeing, following the program. Further improvement in connectedness with nature was noted between the pre-test and the 3-month follow-up, with depression and family functioning approaching significance. For parents under stress, significant improvements were found only in wellbeing after the program. However, additional improvements in anxiety, stress, physical distress, and family conflicts (psychological aggression, corporal punishment, and physical maltreatment) were observed during the follow-up period, with depression and daily functioning approaching significance. Hierarchical regression analysis indicated that connectedness to nature significantly associated with the program's effect on depression. Qualitative analysis revealed that participants benefited from attention restoration, increased awareness, and insights gained from nature and mindfulness practices.

Due to the limitations of the study, including the lack of control group and the use of self-reported measures, future study should verify the benefits of nature-based mindfulness programs particularly on the effects on parents and caregivers under stress and at risk of mental health conditions.

items.title: Physical activity, mental health, and healthy development in adolescents: mechanisms and implications for intervention.
items.authors: Rui L, Zhang J, Li S.

sections.text: Adolescence combines heightened neurobehavioral plasticity with a steep rise in the incidence of depressive and anxiety disorders. Habitual physical activity, by contrast, begins to fall much earlier, from about age seven, so adolescents enter the years of peak diagnostic risk already substantially less active than they were as children. That offset, rather than a coincidence of two curves, is the premise of this review. Meta-analytic syntheses report moderate improvements in depressive (SMD = -0.45, 95% CI -0.59 to -0.31) and anxiety symptoms (SMD = -0.39, 95% CI -0.61 to -0.17) after exercise interventions in samples aged 5 to 18 years, yet several large pragmatic trials have detected no benefit. This mini review synthesizes recent evidence on these effects, the mechanisms proposed to explain them, and why the evidence base remains internally inconsistent. We argue that the contradiction is largely resolvable: efficacy estimates come from a heavily overlapping pool of trials and are inflated by unblinded designs, self-reported outcomes, and passive comparators, whereas universal school-based trials recruit predominantly asymptomatic students and deliver far less activity than prescribed. Mechanisms span three nested levels, neurobiological, psychosocial and behavioral, but most mediation evidence is concurrent rather than temporally ordered. Read through self-determination theory and acceptance-based accounts of distress tolerance, tolerable difficulty appears to be part of how participation confers benefit, with implications for injury, dropout and elite youth sport. Priorities include adequately powered trials with active controls and process evaluation, compositional analysis of movement behaviors, and temporally ordered mechanistic designs.

items.title: Case Report: Intentional massive melatonin ingestion (450 mg) in an adolescent female.
items.authors: Miran S, Amiri B, Astaraki P, Rouzbahani AK.

sections.text: Over-the-counter (OTC) melatonin is widely perceived as benign, yet its unregulated, high-dose formulations create an accessible means of self-harm for adolescents, and reports of intentional overdose have risen alongside a well-documented surge in pediatric exposures. We report a 16-year-old female who intentionally ingested 450 mg of melatonin (90 × 5 mg tablets), a 90-fold supratherapeutic dose, and synthesize this case against the published literature on melatonin overdose, suicidality, and toxicokinetics. She presented 2.5 h post-ingestion with marked somnolence (Glasgow Coma Scale 13/15) and heart rate of 62 beats/min. Venous blood gas showed a mild, respiratory-compensated metabolic acidosis (pH 7.34, HCO3 15.6 mmol/L), with mild hyponatremia and stress leukocytosis. Hepatic, renal, and coagulation studies and a 12-lead electrocardiogram were normal, and a comprehensive toxicology screen was negative, consistent with an isolated exposure (Poison Severity Score Grade 1, Minor). She was medically cleared within 14.5 h of ingestion but, given persistent suicidal ideation on psychiatric evaluation, was transferred to inpatient psychiatric care at 20.5 h post-ingestion. This case, together with a review of published case reports, cohort data, and toxicokinetic evidence, indicates that massive isolated melatonin ingestion typically produces self-limited sedation, consistent with saturable hepatic CYP1A2-mediated clearance, alongside mild, transient metabolic derangement without organ injury. Population-level and case-level evidence converge, however, on a critical message for clinicians: low physiological toxicity does not indicate low psychiatric risk, and every adolescent presenting after intentional OTC chronobiotic ingestion warrants formal psychiatric evaluation regardless of how benign the medical course appears.

items.title: Recreational versus self-medicated cannabis use among adolescents and young adults in Spain: associations with substance use and mental health.
items.authors: Secades-Villa R, Weidberg S, González-Roz A, Alemán-Moussa L, Iza-Fernández C.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Cannabis use is common among adolescents and young adults, yet motives, especially self-medication, remain poorly understood in non-legalized contexts. This study explored differences among recreational, self-medicated, and dual (recreational + self-medicated) cannabis users in sociodemographic, substance use, and mental health characteristics within a large Spanish sample of adolescents and young adults.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Data were collected from 1,078 participants aged 16-30 who reported past-year cannabis use. Based on motives, users were categorized into three groups. Validated measures assessed cannabis use severity, concurrent substance involvement, nicotine dependence, alcohol-related consequences, and mental health. Bivariate analyses and multinomial logistic regressions were performed to identify predictors of group membership.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Dual users comprised most participants (53.2%) and showed the most severe profile, including higher cannabis use frequency, greater scores on the Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (CAST) and the Brief-Marijuana Consequences Questionnaire (B-MACQ), more tobacco co-use, and poorer mental health. Self-medicated users (8.3%) showed greater nicotine dependence, higher risk for cannabis use disorder, and higher scores on the Reality Distortion subscale of the Oviedo Schizotypy Assessment Questionnaire-Abbreviated (ESQUIZO-Q-A) than recreational users (38.5%). Multinomial logistic regressions identified cannabis-related problems and use frequency as the strongest predictors of dual or self-medicated use.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Distinguishing cannabis use motives in adolescents and young adults is crucial, as dual users represent a highly vulnerable subgroup with substance-related and psychological risks. Prevention and intervention efforts should include motive-specific screening, address misconceptions about self-medication, and integrate mental health support, especially amid Spain's evolving cannabis regulations.

items.title: Mental health treatment access among U.S. children according to ASD and ADHD diagnostic status.
items.authors: Alabed ST, Shacker M, Riestra DB, Riestra JM, Hussain NU.
items.journal: PCN reports : psychiatry and clinical neurosciences

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: To compare mental health treatment receipt and difficulty obtaining treatment among U.S. children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) diagnostic status.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We pooled 2023-2024 National Survey of Children's Health data for children aged 3-17 years who received or needed mental health treatment ( N  = 15,952). Children were classified as neither ASD nor ADHD, ADHD only, ASD only, or ASD + ADHD. The reference group included children without diagnosed ASD/ADHD who nevertheless received or needed treatment. The primary outcome was substantial difficulty obtaining treatment. Survey-weighted models adjusted for sociodemographic factors; same-sample sensitivity analyses additionally adjusted for individual clinical conditions and chronic functional limitation.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Substantial difficulty was reported for 22.2%, 23.2%, 28.3%, and 28.2% of the neither, ADHD-only, ASD-only, and ASD + ADHD groups, respectively. ASD + ADHD was associated with higher adjusted odds of difficulty than neither condition (aOR 1.38, 95% CI 1.07-1.78; Bonferroni-adjusted P  = 0.04) but not ASD only (aOR 1.10, 95% CI 0.75-1.59). In the same complete-case sample ( n  = 15,037), the ASD + ADHD estimate was 1.37 (95% CI 1.06-1.78) with sociodemographic adjustment and 0.79 (95% CI 0.59-1.05) after additional adjustment for the individual clinical conditions and chronic functional limitation. Chronic functional limitation was associated with difficulty (aOR 1.89, 95% CI 1.54-2.31).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Differences in difficulty obtaining mental health treatment by ASD/ADHD diagnostic status were attenuated after accounting for measured clinical characteristics and chronic functional limitation. This underscores the importance of considering functional and psychiatric complexity when interpreting access differences across diagnostic groups. Evaluating access should include both treatment receipt and caregiver-reported difficulty obtaining treatment.

items.title: "The significance of context": Fit, friction, and function in the work lives of early career academics with ADHD.
items.authors: Hamilton LG, Ramji AV, Elsherif M, Kapp SK, Sulik J.

sections.text: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is associated with various traits that influence individuals' experiences at work. While some may be experienced as challenging (e.g., when differences in executive function impact time management), others can be more positive (e.g., when curiosity motivates exploration and discovery). Plausibly, academia is a work environment where these positive aspects should be valued. However, ADHD is still often viewed from a medicalised perspective in workplace settings, despite the neurodiversity paradigm offering an alternative, non-pathologising way to frame these individual differences. Research has begun to explore employment experiences and outcomes for adults with ADHD; however, there is currently little data relevant to academic workplaces specifically. This qualitative study offers a critical realist analysis of interviews with early-career academics, seeking to understand first-person ADHD perspectives on establishing an academic career. Consistent with the neurodiversity paradigm, the analysis foregrounds (mis-)matches between individual 'neurotypes' and workplace environments. It also highlights an ecological view by exploring how ADHD matters both for individual careers and for collective knowledge production. Findings suggest that academia can, in principle, be a rewarding environment for ADHDers, though social and institutional pressures often inhibit this potential. Furthermore, having an 'ADHD neurotype' influences both individual career trajectories and wellbeing at work; at the same time, knowledge production at the collective level may benefit from the inclusion of ADHD academics. The findings are discussed in reference to ecological models of neurodiversity and their implications for universities aiming to facilitate neurodivergent contributions and inclusion at work.

items.title: Neuropsychiatric Safety of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists and Tirzepatide in Adults with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus or Obesity.
items.authors: Jani HT, Levine H, Patel A, Trivedi R, Patel XD.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: Neuropsychiatric safety concerns about glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) and tirzepatide prompted regulatory review by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). We synthesized the contemporary evidence in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus or obesity, emphasizing study design, risk of bias, and the distinction between signal detection and causal inference.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus databases were searched without a lower date limit through March 15, 2026 (English, adults ≥18 years). The review was reported with reference to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, and the PRISMA-S and PRISMA-Harms extensions. Evidence was grouped into prespecified categories: randomized syntheses, comparative observational studies and target-trial emulations, outlier non-active-comparator studies, pharmacovigilance analyses, and regulatory reviews. Risk of bias was appraised with the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool and with Risk of Bias in Non-randomised Studies of Interventions; certainty was summarized using Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Twenty studies and two regulatory reviews met the inclusion criteria. Randomized evidence, including two large 2025 meta-analyses and post hoc pooled analyses of semaglutide and tirzepatide, showed no increased risk of suicidality, depression, or anxiety, though psychiatric exclusion criteria limited generalizability. Active-comparator cohorts from the United States, Scandinavia, and the United Kingdom likewise showed no clear increase after confounding control. Passive-comparator and disproportionality analyses generated signals but could not separate drug effects from baseline psychiatric risk, obesity-related distress, or reporting bias. The EMA and FDA conclusions do not support a causal class-wide association between GLP-1 RAs and suicidal ideation or behavior.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Evidence does not support a clinically meaningful increase in neuropsychiatric harm with GLP-1 RAs or tirzepatide in the populations studied. Surveillance remains warranted for patients with substantial psychiatric morbidity, for obesity-only populations, and for long-term rare outcomes.

items.title: The role of PANSS-G12-rated clinical insight in self-reporting the impact of symptoms in patients with schizophrenia living in the community.
items.authors: Frigola-Capell E, González-Caballero JL, Cid J, Romero-López-Alberca C, Ochoa S, Vila-Badia R, Salvador-Carulla L, Moreno-Küstnerh B.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Impaired insight is common in schizophrenia and may influence the interpretation of patient-reported outcome measures, which are increasingly used in patient-centred care and research. However, little is known about how insight relates to self-reported symptom impact. This study examined this relationship in people with schizophrenia in community settings.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Latent class analysis was applied to responses from 162 participants on the Patient-Reported Impact of Symptoms in Schizophrenia (PRISS) scale. Sociodemographic, clinical and functional disability variables were analysed as predictors of class membership. Insight was assessed using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) G12 item in a subset of participants. Invariance analyses evaluated the consistency of the latent class structure across samples and gender.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A four-class model was identified: Low symptom impact (50.62%); Disorganisation (26.54%); Suspiciousness (10.5%); and Severe (12.35%). The Severe clas showed a higher prevalence of clinician-rated negative symptoms. No association was observed between PANSS-G12-rated clinical insight and self-reported negative symptoms. The latent class structure was invariant across samples and gender, although women more frequently reported disturbance of volition, depression and feelings of guilt. Disability, psychological treatment and hospitalisation history were associated with class membership.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Findings suggest that impaired PANSS-G12-rated clinical insight is associated with greater self-reported impact of disorganisation and suspiciousness, but not with the self-reported impact of negative symptoms. Four distinct profiles of symptom impact were identified, with self-reported depression being more prevalent in the most severe profile. These findings may support patient-centred assessment in schizophrenia.

items.title: Adolescent depression and gut microbiota dysbiosis: characteristics, mechanisms, and microbiota-targeted therapeutics.
items.authors: Zi Z, Liu L, Zhou J, Sun Y, Wang N, Liu B, Liu K, Tan Y.

sections.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is one of the most prevalent mental disorders, yet its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood. Accumulating evidence indicates that MDD is closely associated with gut microbiota dysbiosis, with bidirectional communication along the microbiota-gut-brain axis playing a pivotal role in disease development. The gut microbiota and its metabolites exert dual influences on MDD, contributing to its pathophysiology while also offering promising therapeutic targets. In recent years, the prevalence of depression, especially in adolescents, has shown a sharp upward trend, increasing the risk of suicide in this population. However, few studies have systematically reviewed the link between gut dysbiosis and MDD in adolescents. This review summarizes current evidence on structural and functional alterations of the gut microbiota in adolescent MDD and explores the underlying mechanisms mediated by the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Furthermore, we also discuss the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted interventions, including dietary modification, probiotics, prebiotics, synbiotics, postbiotics, and fecal microbiota transplantation. Future research should aim to characterize specific microbial alterations in adolescent MDD and clarify the mechanisms underlying gut-brain interactions, thereby advancing the clinical translation of microbiota-targeted therapeutics for adolescent depression.

items.title: Emotional intensity and visual imagery in trauma nightmares map to posterior hippocampus connectivity.
items.authors: McKenna M, Clancy KJ, So CJ, Pollmann Y, Ren B, Rosso IM.

sections.text: Distressing dreams or nightmares about a traumatic experience are common among trauma-exposed individuals and contribute to the maintenance of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms. Like other intrusive reexperiencing symptoms, trauma-related nightmares are characterized by vivid sensory details and heightened emotional intensity. However, little is known about their underlying neurobiology, and whether it overlaps with that of diurnal reexperiencing symptoms. Therefore, this study aimed to elucidate neurobiological correlates of the phenomenology of trauma-related nightmares. Sixty-six trauma-exposed adults (54 female) completed daily ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) of the phenomenological properties of their trauma-related nightmares for two weeks, as well as resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Pearson correlations examined associations between nightmare properties and functional connectivity within two a priori circuits previously implicated in trauma-related intrusions and episodic memory: 1) an affective circuit between the anterior hippocampus (aHPC) and amygdala (Amyg), and 2) a sensory circuit between the posterior hippocampus (pHPC) and visual cortex (VC). There were no significant associations between nightmare properties and aHPC-Amyg connectivity. In contrast, stronger pHPC-VC connectivity was associated with greater visual detail and emotional intensity of nightmares. These findings align with the established roles of the pHPC and VC in the detailed experience of episodic memory and suggest a novel role for these regions in the affective features of trauma nightmares. Overall, these findings provide support for overlapping neural correlates of the properties of trauma nightmares and diurnal reexperiencing symptoms. They offer additional evidence for a pHPC-VC circuit as a promising neurotherapeutic target for trauma reexperiencing symptoms.

items.title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder With Family Relational Challenges and Persistent Gender-Nonconforming Expression in a Preadolescent Girl: A Case Report.
items.authors: Bazile J, Bernard N, Kaur R, Maganti MK, Faizal KH.

sections.text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in girls may be overlooked or diagnosed late because symptoms can be influenced by emotional dysregulation, compensatory behavior, and family or social context. We describe a 10-year-old girl who was referred for impaired concentration, impulsivity, academic disruption, and aggressive peer interactions. A comprehensive behavioral assessment supported a diagnosis of ADHD, combined presentation. Clinical evaluation also identified substantial conflict involving her parents, twin sister, and grandmother, together with a longstanding pattern of gender-nonconforming expression. Treatment consisted of individual psychotherapy, behavioral parent training, school accommodations, and family-based interventions targeting emotional regulation, executive functioning, and relational conflict. After six months, caregivers and teachers reported fewer aggressive incidents, improved classroom participation, and better emotional regulation, although attentional difficulties persisted. This case illustrates the importance of evaluating ADHD within the child's developmental, educational, and family contexts while distinguishing gender expression from gender identity. Individualized, nonjudgmental, and developmentally appropriate care can address neurodevelopmental impairment without pathologizing a child's personal expression.

items.title: E-MDD: an evidence-guided explainable framework for EEG-based depression recognition.
items.authors: Huang J, Zhang Z, Cao Y, Zhao Z, Niu L.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: An evidence-guided explainable framework, E-MDD, is developed to integrate high-dimensional EEG representations, neurophysiological biomarkers, and large language models for the recognition of EEG-based depression with concise and evidence-based textual explanations.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The proposed E-MDD framework consists of three stages: classification, evidence construction, and evidence-guided inference. In the classification stage, two parallel feature extraction branches are employed to extract Electroencephalography latent features and neurophysiological biomarkers, which are subsequently fused and fed into a lightweight multilayer perceptron for the recognition of depression. In the evidence construction stage, the latent feature dimensions of the EEG are aligned with neurophysiological biomarkers, and the model's decision basis is identified to construct structured evidence supporting the classification results. In the evidence-guided inference stage, structured evidence and the proposed evidence-guided prompt are used to guide the large language model in generating concise textual explanations.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The experimental results on the Mumtaz dataset show that E-MDD achieves an AUC of 0.8472 and an F1-score of 0.8421. Meanwhile, the generated short-text explanations can effectively describe the basis of the model's decision-making for its predictions, demonstrating a high degree of faithfulness. The proposed framework also demonstrates consistent evidence-guided explanation performance across EEGNet and EEGConformer.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Overall, this study proposes a neurophysiologically interpretable framework for EEG-based deep learning models, which effectively enhances the interpretability of deep learning models for depression detection and provides a new perspective for understanding their decision-making mechanisms.

items.title: Causal associations between gut microbiota and autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a two-sample mendelian randomization study.
items.authors: Shi S, Baranova A, Cao H, Zhang F.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The gut microbiota have been implicated in the development of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, the precise causal relationships between the gut microbiota and ASD or ADHD remain unclear.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We investigated potential causal associations between gut microbiota and two neurodevelopmental mental disorders (ASD and ADHD) via Mendelian randomization (MR) analyses. We used genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary datasets, including data from the MiBioGen consortium (N = 18,340), the Dutch Microbiome Project (N = 8,208), an ASD GWAS (N = 46,350), and an ADHD GWAS (N = 292,548).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Our MR analysis identified 16 gut bacterial taxa associated with ASD. Seven taxa were associated with an increased risk (OR 1.03-1.10), while nine were associated with a decreased risk (OR 0.89-0.96). Conversely, 28 gut bacterial taxa were causally linked to ADHD: 16 were associated with an increased risk (OR 1.02-1.04), and 12 were associated with a decreased risk (OR 0.95-0.98). Both ASD and ADHD were causally influenced by the family "Clostridiales noname," but with opposite effects.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Our MR analysis revealed causal effects of specific gut microbiota on ASD and ADHD, suggesting that certain gut microbes may play a role in the development and treatment of these disorders, as well as in their differential diagnosis.

items.title: A systematic review of qualitative research of eating disorders in autistic adults: convergent and divergent experiences.
items.authors: Watts B, Chawner SJRA, Burchell G, Fox JRE.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Autism and eating disorders frequently co-occur, yet relatively little is known about how autistic adults experience eating disorders.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This systematic review synthesised qualitative evidence to explore the lived experiences of autistic adults with an eating disorder and inform autism-informed clinical practice. A systematic search identified 13 eligible studies, which were appraised using the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme (CASP) Qualitative Checklist and synthesised using thematic synthesis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Findings were organised into three themes: eating disorder experiences cannot be understood independently of autistic ways of processing the world; recovery is enabled through developing self-understanding and integrating autism into personal identity; and recovery is facilitated when support aligns with autistic needs rather than neurotypical assumptions. Autistic characteristics, particularly sensory sensitivities, interoceptive differences, and a preference for predictability, fundamentally shaped the development, maintenance, and recovery of eating disorders. Sensory-driven food restriction was frequently experienced independently of body image concerns, highlighting potential conceptual overlap with Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID).

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Autistic adults described eating disorders as inseparable from their autistic experience, indicating the need for a paradigm shift from conceptualising autism and eating disorders as co-occurring conditions towards a model rooted in lived phenomenological experience. Clinical assessment, formulation, and intervention should adopt autism-informed, individualised approaches that recognise sensory processing and interoceptive differences, while future research should examine these mechanisms across a broader range of eating disorder diagnoses.

items.title: The impact of social media use on appearance anxiety among college students -the chain mediating effect of upward social comparison and envy.
items.authors: Lin Y, Li Z, Li L, Lv Z, Song T, Zhou X, Ni J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The widespread adoption of digital media has reshaped young people's aesthetic experiences. The abundance of idealized and digitally enhanced appearance-related content on social media has made appearance anxiety increasingly prevalent among university students. However, the psychological pathways linking social media use to appearance anxiety require systematic examination. This study examined the relationship between social media use and appearance anxiety among university students and tested the chain mediating roles of upward social comparison and envy.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Using convenience sampling, 1,640 university students in China completed the Social Media Use Intensity Scale, Appearance Anxiety Scale, Upward Social Comparison Scale, and Envy Scale. Confirmatory factor analysis, correlation analysis, and PROCESS Model 6 analysis with 5,000 percentile bootstrap samples were used to examine the relationship between social media use and appearance anxiety and the chain mediating effects of upward social comparison and envy. All regression equations controlled for gender, educational level, and average daily social media use time.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: (1) Social media use was significantly and positively associated with appearance anxiety among university students. (2) Upward social comparison mediated the relationship between social media use and appearance anxiety. (3) Envy mediated the relationship between social media use and appearance anxiety. (4) Upward social comparison and envy showed a significant chain mediating effect in the relationship between social media use and appearance anxiety.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This study provided preliminary cross-sectional evidence for an appearance-anxiety-specific comparison-envy pattern linking social media use to appearance anxiety among university students. The findings provide theoretical and practical implications for aesthetic education and media literacy education in higher education within the digital media environment. They may also help guide university students toward more rational aesthetic perceptions, reduced appearance anxiety, and improved physical and mental well-being.

items.title: Adaptation to university life, fear of loneliness, and depression in first-year students at a private university in the Peruvian Amazon: a structural equation model.
items.authors: Gebol-Checàn R, Ascorbe-Peña G, Miguel-Mariño R, Tapullima-Mori C, Cjuno J, Mayta-Llanos J.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: The transition to university is a period of heightened psychological vulnerability. This study aimed to examine the association between adaptation to university life, fear of loneliness, and depression in Peruvian first-year university students.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted with 345 participants selected through non-probability convenience sampling at a single private university in the Peruvian Amazon. The Student Adaptation to College Questionnaire, the Brief Scale of Fear of Loneliness, and the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 were administered, and data were analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The proposed model showed an adequate fit [ χ ² (516) = 1,478, p < 0.001, CFI = 0.940, RMSEA = 0.074, SRMR = 0.069]. Personal-emotional adjustment ( β = 0.49, p < 0.001) and social adjustment (β = 0.29, p = 0.003) were positively associated with fear of loneliness, whereas academic adjustment ( β = -0.34, p < 0.001) and institutional adjustment ( β = -0.22, p = 0.001) were negatively associated; in turn, fear of loneliness was positively related to depression (β = 0.81, p < 0.001). Significant gender differences were found in institutional adjustment [ t (343) = 2.597, p = 0.010, d = 0.29] and personal-emotional adjustment [ t (343) = 3.076, p = 0.002, d = 0.34], with women reporting higher levels than men.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: The findings position fear of loneliness as a key affective link between first-year students' adjustment to university and their depressive symptoms, suggesting that early detection and intervention programs focused on adjustment, implemented during the first year, could help mitigate depression in this population.

items.title: Validation and reliability of the Turkish Binge Eating Disorder Scale: a community-based study.
items.authors: Mengi Çelik Ö, Ağbal Z, Akçakaya SD, Türkmen V, Özdemir M.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: The aim of this study was to evaluate the validity and reliability of the Turkish adaptation of the Binge Eating Disorder Scale (BEDS). Binge eating behavior is a clinically significant condition closely associated with obesity, depression, and emotional dysregulation. Therefore, the adaptation of a psychometrically sound and reliable measurement tool into Turkish holds substantial importance for both clinical and research applications.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Reliability analyses were conducted with 411 adults (67.9% female; mean age = 33.96 ± 12.98 years), while validity analyses were performed with 100 adults. Data were collected through a questionnaire including sociodemographic characteristics, the BEDS, the Binge Eating Scale (BES), and anthropometric measurements. To examine construct validity, exploratory (EFA) and confirmatory factor analyses (CFA) were performed. For reliability analyses, internal consistency (Cronbach's α, McDonald's ω) and test-retest methods were utilized.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Factor analysis indicated that the scale consisted of a single factor and six items, with factor loadings ranging from 0.61 to 0.88. Confirmatory factor analysis demonstrated a good model fit to the data (χ²(13) = 12.420, p = 0.133; χ²/df = 1.553). Cronbach's alpha coefficients for the first and retest administrations were 0.92 and 0.91, respectively, while McDonald's ω coefficients were 0.92 and 0.92, indicating high internal consistency. A strong, positive, and statistically significant correlation was found between BEDS and BES scores (rho = 0.719, p < 0.001), supporting convergent validity. Test-retest reliability assessed using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) demonstrated excellent agreement and temporal stability (ICC = 0.882, 95% CI: 0.825-0.921, p < 0.001).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The Turkish version of the BEDS demonstrated high internal consistency, robust construct validity, and strong overall reliability. The findings suggest that the scale is a valid and reliable tool for assessing binge eating behaviors among Turkish adults. Further studies conducted with diverse sociodemographic groups and clinical samples are recommended to strengthen the generalizability of the instrument.

items.title: Multivariate connectivity deviations reveal task-evoked and clinical network reorganization.
items.authors: Kröll JP, Abdelmotaleb M, Kocataş H, Müller V, Paas L, Meinzer M, Flöel A, Eickhoff S, Patil KR.

sections.text: Understanding how cognitive demands and pathology reshape functional connectivity (FC) requires multivariate, region-specific methods. Here, we introduce one-class SVM-based connectome anomaly recognition (OSCAR), which detects condition-related deviations in regional connectivity profiles. OSCAR learns region-to-whole-brain connectivity patterns from a reference state using one-class support vector machines and quantifies target-condition deviations based on outlier proportions. We validated OSCAR across three diverse cognitive tasks, in which it identified regions within networks associated with conflict processing, object-location memory, and lexical learning. In a clinical cohort that included individuals with early psychosis, OSCAR identified relevant regions, including thalamic and basal ganglia areas. Compared with permutation-based multivariate analysis of variance, OSCAR detected additional established task- and disease-relevant parcels, while its task-related findings were at least as close, and often closer, to independent activation findings. OSCAR thus provides an interpretable, region-centered approach for mapping multivariate FC reconfigurations across experimental and clinical conditions.

items.title: Academic stress and internet gaming addiction in college students: a moderated mediation model with anxiety as mediator and peer support as moderator.
items.authors: Li J, Liu B, Wang Y.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Academic stress is a known risk factor for internet gaming addiction among college students; however, the underlying mechanisms remain not fully elucidated. The current study aimed to examine the mediating role of anxiety in the relationship between academic stress and internet gaming addiction, as well as the moderating role of peer support.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 636 Chinese college students in China. Participants completed measures of academic stress, anxiety, peer support, and internet gaming addiction. Analyses were performed using the PROCESS macro for SPSS. Model 4 was used to test mediation, and Model 59 was used to test moderated mediation, with age and gender controlled for in all analyses.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Academic stress was positively associated with internet gaming addiction among college students ( r  = 0.28, p  < 0.001), and anxiety mediated this relationship (indirect effect = 0.22, 95% CI = [0.16, 0.27]). Peer support significantly moderated this indirect effect by buffering the path from academic stress to anxiety ( b  = -0.18, p  <.01). Specifically, for college students with lower peer support, the relationship between academic stress and anxiety was significant ( b  = 0.42, p  <.001); for those with higher peer support, the relationship remained significant but weaker ( b  = 0.24, p  <.001).

sections.heading: Conclusion

items.title: Association between uncertainty regarding malignant risk and anxiety in patients with pulmonary nodules: a serial mediation analysis of illness perception and rumination.
items.authors: Wu S, Liu M, Yi S, Wang R, Song Z, Xie F, Chen W, Qu H, Huang Y.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This study examined the relationship between uncertainty regarding the risk of malignancy after pulmonary nodule detection and anxiety, and the serial indirect effects of illness perception and ruminative thinking.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A total of 308 patients with pulmonary nodules who were admitted to our hospital between January 2023 and January 2026 were included in the study. General information was collected, and participants were assessed using the MUIS, BBIPQ, RRS, and the Chinese version of the GAD-7. Correlation and serial indirect effect analyses were performed using SPSS 26.0 and the PROCESS macro (Model 6). Bootstrap resampling with 5,000 samples was used to assess the stability of indirect effects.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Among the 308 patients with pulmonary nodules, the MUIS scores ranged from 24 to 86, with a mean of 56.10 ± 12.21. The BIPQ scores ranged 3 to76, with a mean of 43.26 ± 10.67, the RRS scores ranged from 22 to 72, with a mean of 44.66 ± 10.60, and the GAD-7 scores ranged from 1 to16, with a mean of 8.84 ± 2.62. No significant differences in GAD-7 scores were observed among patients with different demographic or disease characteristics ( P >0.05). Pearson's correlation analysis showed that MUIS scores were positively correlated with BIPQ, RRS and GAD-7 scores ( r  = 0.687, 0.577, and 0.745, P  < 0.05). BIPQ score was positively correlated with RRS and GAD-7 score ( r  = 0.577; 0.601, P  < 0.05). RRS score was positively correlated with GAD-7 score ( r  = 0.574, P  < 0.05). The MUIS had a significant direct effect on GAD-7, accounting for 75.63% of the total effect. The indirect effect consists of three paths: ① MUIS → RRS → GAD-7, with an indirect effect of 0.014, accounting for 8.75% of the total effect; ② MUIS → BIPQ → GAD-7, with an indirect effect of 0.016, accounting for 10.00% of the total effect; and ③ MUIS → BIPQ → RRS → GAD-7, with an indirect effect of 0.009, accounting for 5.62% of the total effect.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: After pulmonary nodule detection, uncertainty regarding the risk of malignancy is positively associated with anxiety, partly explained by the serial indirect effects of illness perception and ruminative thinking, consistent with the hypothesized model.

items.title: Beyond criminal intent: infant-directed violence as a symptom of postpartum psychosis.
items.authors: Laufer B.

sections.text: Postpartum psychosis is a rare but severe psychiatric emergency in which infant-directed violence, although uncommon, is best understood as a manifestation of acute psychotic illness rather than enduring maternal hostility or conventional criminal intent. The psychotic content of postpartum psychosis is often infant focus, with profound disturbances in reality testing that transform the mother's perception of her infant, framing the child through delusions and hallucinations as an object of danger, salvation, contamination, or divine significance. In the cases of infanticide or filicide, the violence directed at the child, although objectively tragic are subjectively protective or morally necessary. Drawing on the existing literature on postpartum psychotic phenomenology, this conceptual analysis uses two contrasting clinical cases as illustrative examples-one involving infanticide and one without infant-directed violence-to examine how infant-focused delusions can shape perception and behavior. By contrasting these cases, the article demonstrates how infant-focused delusions directly dictate behavior and explores why the infant becomes the primary object of the mother's psychotic experience. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of this comparative framework for forensic assessment, criminal responsibility, violence risk evaluation, and clinical intervention.
